newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Formosa Plastics says won't give up China project.
newsitem.headline: Formosa Plastics says won't give up China project.

text.p: Formosa Plastics group pledged on Thursday to build a controversial US$3 billion power plant in mainland China, Taiwan's arch-rival, even if it has to wait a year for Taipei's approval.
"We will not give up our mainland project," a spokesman for the Taiwan petrochemical giant told Reuters by telephone.
"A U.S. firm in which we have a three percent stake has sent funds to finance the site work, including blasting off a hill, to prepare for the plant's construction," he said.
Mainland officials were on hand to oversee the site work.
The official quoted group chairman Wang Yung-ching as saying the group would patiently await Taiwan's approval of the project even if it meant waiting for "six months or one year".
If Taipei still had not approved the project after a year, Formosa would consider selling its interest to a foreign consortium, the Formosa spokesman said.

Formosa announced in June 1996 that it and China's coastal Fujian province would build a 3,600-megawatt thermal power plant in Fujian's Zhangzhou city in what, at US$3 billion, would have been the biggest Taiwan investment in China.
Formosa sought Taiwan's approval but said two months later it had backed out after President Lee Teng-hui urged local firms to slow their China investments.
On March 29, Wang caught Taiwan's Nationalist government off guard on when he said construction already had begun.
Taipei reacted by warning against any unauthorised Taiwan investment on the mainland -- even through overseas affiliates -- and saying Formosa's project would not be approved.
Wang initially appeared to have backed down, issuing a statement on March 31 saying Formosa would respect Taiwan's decision and drop the project if approval were denied.

Taiwan's Republic of China government, driven from the mainland after losing a civil war to the communists in 1949, bans direct mainland investments but has allowed a wide range of "indirect" projects as long as they have Taipei's approval.
Major projects in infrastructure, finance and other sensitive areas remain forbidden to ensure Taiwan does not become vulnerable through over-reliance on China's economy.

Wang, a political maverick with huge influence as head of Taiwan's top conglomerate, was quoted by Taipei's China Times as saying that investing in the mainland should not be interpreted by Taipei as "financially helping the Chinese communists".

"It's normal that we (Taiwan) react negatively when the mainland creates political or diplomatic problems for us," he said. "But if Taiwan refrains from mainland contacts, what becomes of the nation's internationalisation policy?"

Wang said internationalisation was an inevitable trend and that Taiwan must not become isolated. As Taiwan becomes a member of the international community, its policy of rejecting major mainland projects would become impossible.
